title: French Toast
subtitle: Eggy bread fried in butter with cinnamon and maple syrup
excerpt: Thick slices of white bread soaked in a spiced egg-and-milk custard, then fried in butter until deep golden on both sides. Served with maple syrup and fresh berries or a dusting of icing sugar.

recipe.sourceNotes: French toast (pain perdu in French, eggy bread in British households) is one of the oldest ways of using up stale bread. It appears in a 4th-century Roman cookery text as a dish of bread soaked in milk, fried in oil, and served with honey. The modern American version, which became the international standard, uses thick-cut bread with cinnamon in the custard and maple syrup as the topping. Day-old or slightly stale bread works better than fresh because it absorbs the custard without falling apart.

recipeTools.notes: A wide non-stick or cast-iron pan.

content.text: Stale bread absorbs the custard better than fresh without going soggy. Soak each slice for 30 seconds per side: enough to absorb but not so long that the bread falls apart. Use enough butter to properly coat the pan and help the bread colour evenly on both sides.
Whisk the eggs, milk, cinnamon, vanilla, and sugar together in a shallow bowl wide enough to fit a bread slice.
Dip each bread slice into the egg mixture, letting it soak for 20 to 30 seconds per side. The bread should feel saturated but not falling apart.
Melt half the butter in a large non-stick pan over medium heat. Cook 2 slices at a time for 2 to 3 minutes per side until deeply golden. Add the remaining butter for the second batch.
Serve immediately with maple syrup and a dusting of icing sugar if desired. Fresh berries alongside are a good addition.
